question: May a New York notary certify a copy of a document as a true copy?

options.text: No; New York notaries have no authority to certify copies
options.why: Correct. The custodian of the original issues certified copies; a notary can't.
Wrong. That's allowed in some states, but not New York.
Wrong. Vital records come from the issuing agency.

options.text: Yes, if they compare it to the original
options.why: Wrong. Comparing doesn't create authority.

explanation: A New York notary has no power to certify a copy as true.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Certified Copy)

refs.title: Definitions: Certified Copy (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: May a New York notary perform a marriage ceremony?

options.why: Correct. New York notaries aren't authorized to solemnize marriages.
Wrong. Florida allows it; New York doesn't.
Wrong. The license doesn't empower the notary.
Wrong. No geographic exception.

explanation: New York notaries have no authority to perform marriages.
source: N.Y. Dom. Rel. Law §11; DOS Notary Public License Law

refs.title: N.Y. Dom. Rel. Law §11 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 13)

question: Which powers does Executive Law §135 give a New York notary?

options.text: Administer oaths and affirmations, take affidavits and depositions, take acknowledgments and proofs, and protest negotiable instruments
options.why: Correct. Executive Law §135 lists these powers: oaths, affirmations, affidavits, depositions, acknowledgments, proofs and protests.
Wrong. Apostilles are issued by the Department of State, not notaries.
Wrong. Deeds are recorded by the county clerk.
Wrong. Only courts can grant divorces.

explanation: §135 authorizes oaths, affirmations, affidavits, depositions, acknowledgments, proofs and protests.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §135 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)

question: A non-attorney notary is asked to supervise the execution of a will. What is the risk?

options.text: Supervising a will execution can be the unauthorized practice of law and, if done wrong, can make the will invalid
options.why: Correct. Will execution has strict formalities that are a matter for attorneys; a notary who supervises it risks the unauthorized practice of law and an invalid will.

options.text: No risk; notaries handle wills routinely
options.why: Wrong. Notaries may notarize certain will-related affidavits but shouldn't direct will executions.
Wrong. Executors are named in the will or appointed by the court, not created by notarization.
Wrong. Notarizing never changes one type of instrument into another.

explanation: Non-attorney notaries should not supervise will executions; it can be practicing law and risks an invalid will.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Wills; Professional Conduct)

refs.title: Wills (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 14)
Professional Conduct (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: A signer can't speak English, and the notary doesn't speak the signer's language. What should the notary consider?

options.text: Whether the notary can communicate directly enough to identify the signer and confirm willingness; if not, decline or refer to a notary who speaks the language
options.why: Correct. The notary must be able to perform the act properly.

options.text: Always use the signer's child as an interpreter
options.why: Wrong. A family interpreter may have an interest and could misstate things.
Wrong. Gestures may not establish understanding.
Wrong. Translating legal documents isn't the notary's role.

explanation: If the notary can't communicate with the signer, they should refer them to a notary who can.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.3 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 16)

question: A notary is asked to notarize a photograph. What should they do?

options.text: Notarize only a signature on a written statement about the photo (e.g. an affidavit), not the photo itself
options.why: Correct. Notaries certify signatures and oaths, not images.
Wrong. That certifies nothing meaningful.

options.text: Certify the photo as a true copy
options.why: Wrong. New York notaries can't certify copies.
Wrong. A signed statement can be notarized.

explanation: The notary can notarize a signer's sworn statement about a photo, not the photo itself.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions)

refs.title: Definitions: Jurat (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 20)

question: A hospitalized signer is heavily sedated. Family members urge the notary to proceed. The notary should:

options.text: Decline or postpone until the signer is aware and able to act willingly
options.why: Correct. Awareness and willingness are essential.
Wrong. The family's wishes don't replace the signer's capacity.
Wrong. A witness doesn't cure incapacity.
Wrong. That would be forgery.

explanation: A notary must not proceed if the signer lacks awareness.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.3 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 16)

question: Who appoints a 'commissioner of deeds' in New York City?

options.why: Correct. Commissioners of deeds in NYC are appointed by the City Clerk and have limited powers.
Wrong. That's for notaries.
Wrong. Not the appointing authority.
Wrong. Not the appointing authority.

explanation: In New York City, commissioners of deeds are appointed by the City Clerk.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §140 (commissioners of deeds, NYC) (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)

question: A customer brings a deed already signed and asks for a jurat 'because it's faster'. The deed will be recorded. What should the notary do?

options.text: Not choose for them; explain that deeds are usually acknowledged and let the customer or their attorney decide
options.why: Correct. The notary can describe the acts but shouldn't make the legal choice.
Wrong. It may make the deed unrecordable, and choosing the act carelessly risks legal harm.
Wrong. Unrequested acts may confuse the record.
Wrong. The notary can still help once the customer decides.

explanation: Recordable deeds generally need an acknowledgment; the notary should leave the choice to the customer or their attorney.
source: NY DOS Notary Public License Law (Definitions: Acknowledgment; Professional Conduct)

refs.title: Definitions: Acknowledgment (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 19)
Professional Conduct (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: A notary visiting New Jersey is asked to notarize there under their New York commission. The notary should:

options.text: Decline; a New York commission doesn't authorize acts in New Jersey
options.why: Correct. Authority ends at the state line.

options.text: Notarize, since the signer is a New Yorker
options.why: Wrong. The signer's residence doesn't extend the notary's authority.

options.text: Notarize if the document will be used in New York
options.why: Wrong. Where the act takes place is what counts.

options.text: Notarize and write 'New York' as the venue
options.why: Wrong. That would be a false venue.

explanation: A traditional New York notarization must be performed in New York.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §130 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 5)

question: May a New York notary take a deposition?

options.why: Correct. §135 authorizes notaries to take depositions.
Wrong. It's a listed power.
Wrong. Depositions are usually taken without a judge.
Wrong. Depositions are mostly civil.

explanation: Executive Law §135 authorizes notaries to take depositions.

refs.title: N.Y. Exec. Law §135 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 7)
CPLR Rule 3113 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 13)

question: A signer who can't write makes an 'X' mark as a signature. What is the prudent practice?

options.text: Have the mark made in the notary's presence and witnessed, with the signer's name written near the mark, and note it in the record
options.why: Correct. Witnessing and labeling the mark documents who made it.
Wrong. Signatures by mark are recognized.

options.text: Sign the signer's full name for them
options.why: Wrong. That would be forgery.
Wrong. You can't verify who made it.

explanation: Signatures by mark should be made in the notary's presence, witnessed, labeled with the signer's name and recorded.

refs.title: 19 NYCRR §182.9 (NY DOS Notary Public License Law, p. 18)
